title: What a Responsible Breeder Actually Looks Like
body:
Dog breeding keeps showing up in Nigerian papers lately, usually framed around its upside: jobs, security, a real economic activity rather than a hobby. Whatever you make of that framing, it's worth pausing on a plainer question underneath it, one that matters a lot more to anyone actually looking for a puppy than any national-growth argument does. What separates a responsible breeder from someone who is just producing puppies to sell?

Daily Paws put together a practical checklist on exactly this, and most of it holds up anywhere, Nigeria included. A responsible breeder tends to keep litters small and infrequent rather than running a constant churn. They screen for health issues common to the breed instead of leaving that to chance. They ask the buyer questions too, about living space, experience, who else is in the home, rather than selling to whoever shows up with cash first. And they're generally willing to show you where the puppies actually live, let you meet the mother, and take a dog back later if things don't work out. None of that is complicated. It just takes more effort than listing a litter and waiting for the fastest payment.

That effort is exactly where the responsibility sits for anyone using a directory like PetMatch, too. Breeder listings here are self-reported, the same as every other listing, and PetMatch doesn't independently verify health records, vaccination history, or breeding credentials behind any of them. That's not a gap we're trying to hide; it's in the FAQ, plainly, because pretending otherwise would be worse than saying it outright. The signs above are the ones worth checking for yourself before anything is agreed, not the platform's job to confirm on your behalf.

In practice, that means meeting the breeder and the litter in person rather than over a single WhatsApp thread, asking directly for vaccination and health records instead of taking a description on faith, and treating any reluctance to let you do either as the actual red flag, more telling than anything written in a listing. A longer rundown on meeting safely is at https://petmatch.fit/safety.

Whether dog breeding in Nigeria grows into the formal economic activity those recent pieces describe, or stays what it still mostly is, a smaller arrangement between neighbors who know each other's dogs, that one question doesn't change with scale: who's doing the harder asking, the buyer or the breeder. It's worth being the one asking.
